title: Praying with the qazi
hook: tradition says that at prayer he told the qazi his mind had wandered home to a young horse
carry: where is your mind right now

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sultanpur, and one sentence: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Beneath the labels, people.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS AFTER — BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: A place of worship, and words you know by heart. Your body knows exactly when to stand and when to bow. And your mind? It's in the parking lot. Did I lock the car? It's in tomorrow's meeting, replaying an argument from last week. Anyone who has prayed, meditated or even tried to listen to a friend knows this. The body shows up. The mind wanders off. Five hundred years ago in Sultanpur, the story goes, a religious judge had exactly that happen, at exactly the wrong moment, standing next to exactly the wrong person.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS WHEN TO BOW.` → `THE MIND IS IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `SULTANPUR, AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis tell it this way. Word of Nanak's sentence reached the governor, Daulat Khan, and the qazi, the town's Muslim judge. They called him in. If there is no Hindu and no Muslim, they said, then come and pray with us. It was Friday. Nanak went with them to the mosque. The governor and the qazi bowed, and Nanak stood quietly and didn't join in. Afterward the qazi was indignant: you came to pray with us, and you didn't pray. Nanak answered gently: who was I supposed to pray with? The governor's mind was far away in Kabul, buying horses. The qazi's was at home, where a mare had just given birth, worrying that the foal might wander off and fall into the open well in the courtyard. Both men were silent, the story says, because it was true. Hear what this story isn't. It isn't mocking Muslim prayer, or any prayer. Muslim teachers have long stressed that prayer needs a present heart, humble attention; the Arabic word is khushu. Nanak's point sits right beside theirs. Tradition connects the moment with a hymn of Nanak's in the scripture on what makes a true Muslim. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest living your holy book. His challenge was never to stop praying. It was to actually be there when you do. That's why the story stings. Anyone who prays has been the qazi, standing in the right place with the mind at home by the well.
screen: `THEN COME AND PRAY WITH US.` · `THE MIND IN KABUL. THE MIND BY THE WELL.` · `NOT MOCKERY. A PRESENT HEART.` · `LET MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · then, large: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND RIGHT NOW?`

segments.voice: If you pray, say one short prayer you know from your own tradition, slowly, meaning every word. If you don't, rest your whole mind on your breath, or on one sound in the room. When the mind wanders to the car, the meeting, the well, notice where it went and bring it back, without scolding.
Qazi. The Muslim judge of Sultanpur whose mind, Nanak said, had wandered home to a young horse while he stood at prayer.
Your line: where is your mind right now. Tomorrow, the friend with the rebab. That's day thirty.
